idiom_name: url::Url link values + serde carrier struct + reqwest::Client dereference
implementation_notes: Rust std has no URI type and no HTTP client, so the classic hand-written link structure is replaced by the ecosystem pair: the url crate's Url is a parsed WHATWG-Standard URL record (Url::parse returns Result<Url, ParseError>, base.join() resolves relative references against a base URL), and with its serde feature enabled Url serializes as a plain string, making it a first-class field in the carrier struct that serde_json moves across the boundary (axum/actix-web response body, message payload). The producer embeds typed Link structs (rel, href: Url, method) in the output; the consumer dereferences with reqwest::Client::get(link.href).send(), where Response::url() reports the final URL after redirects and Response::error_for_status() turns a dead link's 404 into an Err. The classic manual form - a String href parsed ad hoc at each hop - is justified only where the url/reqwest dependency is unacceptable (no_std or embedded targets); elsewhere the parsed Url value is preferred because it validates once at the boundary instead of at every dereference.
pitfalls: Borrows cannot be the carrier: serde requires owned data, so a forwarded &T/Rc reference to the resource simply fails to compile - the Rust-specific failure is the opposite of a dangling pointer: converting Url back to String at layer boundaries and re-parsing untrusted input at every hop, losing the one-time boundary validation.

Url::parse rejects relative references outright (ParseError::RelativeUrlWithoutBase); storing or forwarding hrefs that are only valid against a base breaks at dereference time - resolve with base.join() at the producer and transfer absolute URLs.

Dereferencing a link synchronously (reqwest::blocking or any blocking I/O) inside a tokio worker stalls the whole runtime; use the async Client and share one clone-cheap Client instead of building one per request.

Following a link is not authorization: URL parsing normalizes but never validates the target, so a link from an untrusted response can redirect the client to internal addresses (SSRF) - check scheme/host against an allowlist and configure the Client's redirect::Policy before dereferencing.
error_for_status is opt-in: send() returns Ok(Response) even when a dead link yields a 404, so a consumer that skips Response::status()/error_for_status() silently deserializes an error body.
cannot-be-a-base URLs (data:, mailto:) have no slash-separated path and reject join()-style resolution - check Url::cannot_be_a_base() before path-based link construction.
